title: Ellicott's Commentary for English Readers
author: Charles John Ellicott (ed.)
allowedUseNotes: Public-domain 19th-century commentary (published 1878-1879, long pre-1928, editor died 1905). May be cited, quoted in short excerpt, or paraphrased freely with attribution; no full-chapter reproduction needed per this project's own tighter internal policy regardless.
summary: A Victorian-era verse-by-verse commentary for a general English readership, edited by Charles John Ellicott (Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol) with contributions from multiple named clergy-scholars of the period. On 2 Samuel 3:7, the commentary reads Ish-bosheth's accusation against Abner (going in to Rizpah, Saul's concubine) through the ancient Near Eastern convention that a king's harem was considered the property of his successor, so that taking a woman from it functioned as an assertion of a claim to the throne — a reading the commentary cross-references against the same convention elsewhere in the David narrative (2 Samuel 12:8, 16:21-22; 1 Kings 2:13-25). The commentary also notes, on the same verse, that the accusation's political weight does not itself establish that Abner intended such a claim, since he was at the time actively working to maintain Ish-bosheth on the throne rather than to displace him — a caution consistent with this project's own narrated-not-adjudicated framing of claim-abner-break, that the text does not itself confirm whether the accusation was true.
